::: {.lead}
The *Sunrise* shop has new opening hours from 1 December. Huda, the office
manager, must tell the whole staff at Monday's meeting, with a few slides
on the big screen. The first try is one slide with seven long sentences in
small black letters. Nobody at the back can read it, and everybody reads
instead of listening. In this lesson you make clear slides in
**PowerPoint**: you choose a **layout**, give the talk one look with a
**theme**, keep **few words** on each slide and the rest in the **speaker
notes**, and add a quiet **transition** and an **animation**. These notes
are a short reference: in class you try each idea in PowerPoint, as an
experiment of the **worksheet**.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary slide-layout placeholder theme designer colour-contrast slide-show speaker-notes slide-transition slide-animation >}}

## 8.1 Slides and layouts

PowerPoint opens with a window of three parts: the slide thumbnails on the
left, the big slide in the middle and the notes pane under it
(@fig-window).

![The PowerPoint window and its tabs.](images/ppt-window.png){#fig-window width=100%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.1 — Layout and placeholder"}
A **layout** is the plan of a slide: where the title, the text and the
pictures go. Each layout has **placeholders**, dashed boxes that say "Click
to add title" or "Click to add text". You click a placeholder and type.
:::

![Four common layouts.](images/layouts.png){#fig-layouts width=100%}

- **Home › New Slide** adds a slide; the arrow under it lets you choose the
  layout.
- **Home › Layout** changes the layout of the slide you are on.
- The first slide uses **Title Slide**; most slides use **Title and
  Content**; **Two Content** puts a list next to a picture.
- A picture works as in Word (Lecture 4): resize it from a corner, and
  write its alt text.
- **File › Save As** › `shop-hours.pptx`. Press **F5** to start the slide
  show and **Esc** to stop it.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.1 — Huda's first two slides"}
1. Slide 1, *Title Slide*: "New shop hours", and under it "Huda, Office
   Manager".
2. Home › New Slide › *Title and Content*: the title "From 1 December" and
   three points in the content placeholder.
3. Huda saves the file as `shop-hours.pptx`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Drawing your own text boxes on a Blank slide. Then the titles jump from
slide to slide, and Designer cannot use them. Use the placeholders of a
layout.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/slide-builder.html" poster="sims/slide-builder.png" title="Slide Builder: one good slide" height="820" >}}

*In class: Experiment 1 of the worksheet, the layouts of a short talk, a new Two Content slide and the slide show.*

## 8.2 One look for the whole talk: themes and Designer

Huda's slides are black on white. A **theme** gives all of them the same
colours and fonts in one click (@fig-themes).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.2 — Theme and Designer"}
A **theme** is a set of colours, fonts and backgrounds for all slides
(**Design** tab). **Designer** (**Design › Designer**, in Microsoft 365)
suggests designs for the slide you are on; you click one to use it.
:::

![One slide in three themes.](images/themes.png){#fig-themes width=100%}

- **Design** tab › click a theme; the arrow on the right shows more.
- **Variants** (next to the themes) change the colours of the same theme.
- The text must be easy to read: dark text on a light background, or light
  text on a dark background. This is strong **colour contrast**.
- Designer needs an Internet connection; if it is not there, use the
  layouts.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.2 — A theme for the hours"}
1. Huda clicks the Design tab and chooses an orange theme like *Sunrise*.
2. Both slides change at once: orange titles, a light background, the same
   font.
3. On slide 2, Huda opens Designer and picks one of its designs.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A different colour and font on every slide, or light grey text on a light
background. The talk looks messy, and people at the back cannot read it.
:::

*In class: Experiment 2 of the worksheet, a theme for the whole talk, two variants and the contrast.*

## 8.3 Few words on the slide, the rest in the notes

The slide helps the speaker; it does not replace the speaker
(@fig-text).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.3 — Few words and speaker notes"}
Each slide has **one idea**, a short title and **3 to 5 points**, each of a
few words (about 8 or fewer). The details are what you **say**: write them
in the **speaker notes**, the notes pane under the slide. In the slide
show, **Presenter View** shows the notes only to you.
:::

![Seven sentences or four short points.](images/text-amount.png){#fig-text width=100%}

- The text is big enough to read from the back: about 24 pt or more.
- **View › Notes** shows the notes pane when you do not see it.
- Notes are short reminders, not a text to read aloud.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.3 — From seven sentences to four points"}
1. Huda's first slide has seven long sentences.
2. Huda keeps four points: "Sun–Thu: 9:00–20:00", "Friday: closed",
   "Saturday: 10:00–18:00", "From 1 December".
3. "Tell every customer" and "Rana puts a notice on the door" go into the
   speaker notes: they are things to say, not things on the slide.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Making the font smaller so that all sentences fit. The problem is too much
text, not a too big font.
:::

*In class: Experiment 3 of the worksheet, a slide of six long points made short, with the details in the speaker notes.*

## 8.4 Movement: transitions and animations

Huda's slides change with a jump, and all the points appear at once, so the
staff read ahead. A quiet **transition** and a simple **animation** help
the audience follow (@fig-transitions, @fig-animation).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 8.4 — Transition and animation"}
A **transition** is the way one slide changes to the next in the slide show
(**Transitions** tab: Fade, Push, Wipe …). An **animation** makes one thing
on a slide appear or move (**Animations** tab: Appear, Fade …).
:::

![Transitions: quiet and the same on every slide.](images/transitions.png){#fig-transitions width=100%}

![An animation: the points come one by one, on a click.](images/animation-steps.png){#fig-animation width=100%}

- **Transitions** tab › Fade › **Duration** 0.5–1 second › **Apply To
  All**: the same quiet change on every slide.
- Select the list › **Animations** tab › **Appear** or **Fade** › **Effect
  Options › By Paragraph**: the points come one by one, on a click.
- Use few effects: one quiet transition for the talk, and an animation only
  where points should come one by one.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.4 — Huda's slides move"}
1. Huda opens the Transitions tab, clicks **Fade**, sets 0.7 seconds and
   clicks **Apply To All**.
2. On slide 2, she selects the three points and clicks **Animations ›
   Fade**, then **Effect Options › By Paragraph**.
3. In the slide show, every click shows the next hour, and the staff listen
   to one point at a time.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A different wild transition on every slide, and points that fly and spin.
The audience watches the effects, not the message.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/transition-lab.html" poster="sims/transition-lab.png" title="Transition Lab: transitions and animations" height="700" >}}

*In class: Experiment 4 of the worksheet, one Fade for every slide, and three points that appear one by one.*

## Case study: Slide Doctor

Huda's colleagues send slides for the Monday meeting, and each slide has
one problem: seven long sentences, light grey text on light blue, a photo of
the shop that is too tall and thin, a photo without alt text, and a
"Thank you!" slide in the wrong layout. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses these slides. In the mini-game below you choose the
best fix for each one.

(support.microsoft.com).

## Exercises

1. What is a layout?
2. What is a placeholder?
3. Which layout fits the first slide of a talk?
4. Where do you choose a theme?
5. Why is light grey text on a light background a problem?
6. How many points should a slide have?
7. Where do you write what you will say?
8. What is a transition? On which tab is it?
9. What is an animation? Give one example.
10. Which button gives every slide the same transition?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The plan of a slide: where the title, the text and the pictures go.
2. A dashed box of a layout where you click and type or add a picture.
3. Title Slide.
4. On the Design tab.
5. The contrast is weak: people at the back cannot read it.
6. About 3 to 5 short points.
7. In the speaker notes, the notes pane under the slide.
8. The way one slide changes to the next in the slide show; the Transitions tab.
9. An effect that makes one thing on a slide appear or move; for example, the points of a list appear one by one.
10. Apply To All.
:::
